No account access required.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "daaff2b9-1e0d-46a0-ad0f-120b90348ddd", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "For a resource type that changes many times per day, **daily recording mode is almost always cheaper**, and it's not particularly close.

**Why:**

AWS Config bills per configuration item (CI) recorded, regardless of mode:

- **Continuous recording** writes a new configuration item every time AWS Config detects a change to the resource. If a resource type changes dozens or hundreds of times a day (e.g., an Auto Scaling group constantly scaling, an EC2 instance with frequently changing tags, or ECS tasks churning), you get billed for *every single one* of those change events.
- **Daily recording** collapses all changes to a resource into a single configuration item per day, capturing only the latest state at the end of the recording period — no matter how many times it actually changed. You're billed for one CI per resource per day, flat.

So the cost driver is CI *volume*: continuous mode's cost scales linearly with change frequency, while daily mode's cost is constant (one CI/resource/day) no matter how "noisy" the resource is. For a high-churn resource type, that difference compounds fast — e.g., a resource changing 50 times/day costs ~50x more under continuous than under daily.

**The tradeoff:** daily mode sacrifices granularity — you lose the full change history and point-in-time configuration timeline within that day, which matters if you rely on Config for detailed audit trails, compliance evidence of every state transition, or fine-grained drift detection tied to specific change events. If you only care about "what did this look like as of end of day," daily is the cheaper, still-useful choice for chatty resource types.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
